name: The Honest Scorecard
why_it_works: Every comparison chart where one side wins every row looks rigged. Admitting one row where the typical option wins makes every other row believable, because conceding a point is something only a confident, honest brand would do.

hook.pattern: Promise a comparison chart where you don't win every row.
examples: {{brand}} vs the usual way. We lose one row. Honestly.
A comparison chart where we don't win everything.
Before you choose a {{service}}, score them on these five things.

variables.name: row_one
variables.description: First criterion and the honest result
variables.example: Someone answers when you have a claim: us

variables.name: row_two
variables.description: Second criterion and the honest result
variables.example: Policies compared across several carriers: us

variables.name: row_three
variables.description: Third criterion and the honest result
variables.example: Yearly review without you asking: us

variables.name: losing_row
variables.description: The row the typical option honestly wins
variables.example: Fastest at 2 a.m. with no conversation: buying online wins

slides.headline: A chart where we don't win everything
slides.visual_prompt: Clean scorecard graphic with two column headers, {{brand}} and a generic option, empty rows, {{brand}} colors, 4:5

slides.headline: Row 1
slides.visual_prompt: Scorecard row with a check mark in the {{brand}} column, simple icon of a phone being answered, flat design, 4:5

slides.headline: Row 2
slides.visual_prompt: Scorecard row with a check mark in the {{brand}} column, icon of documents side by side, flat design, 4:5

slides.headline: Row 3
slides.visual_prompt: Scorecard row with a check mark in the {{brand}} column, calendar icon, flat design, 4:5

slides.headline: Row 4: they win this one
slides.body: {{losing_row}}. If that matters most, go that way.
slides.visual_prompt: Scorecard row with the check mark in the generic column instead, highlighted with a small honest-badge sticker, flat design, 4:5

slides.headline: Why we showed you that
slides.body: A chart where one side wins everything is an ad, not a comparison.
slides.visual_prompt: Warm photo of a {{brand}} team member at a desk, open friendly posture, natural light, 4:5

slides.headline: The final score
slides.body: 3 to 1. You decide what matters to you.
slides.visual_prompt: Completed scorecard graphic showing 3 checks for {{brand}} and 1 for the generic option, clean layout, 4:5

slides.headline: Score us yourself
slides.visual_prompt: {{brand}} logo card with the offer in large type, brand colors, plenty of white space, 4:5

craft.notes: Put the losing row fourth, after three wins, so it reads as honesty rather than weakness. Give it the same visual weight as the wins; hiding it in small type ruins the effect. Close by handing the decision back to the viewer.

do_not: Name a real competitor in any column
Pick a fake weakness (like 'we care too much'); the conceded row must be real
Claim any row you can't back up if a customer asks
compliance: Insurance: include the licensed agency name and state license number; say coverage and pricing vary by policy and carrier; no 'best rates' claims without proof
Financial advisors: no performance, return or income promises; include required firm and registration disclosures; comparisons must be fair and balanced per your regulator's advertising rules
Personal trainers: no guaranteed body or health results
